title: Why Allowing Your Students To Talk Can Be An Effective Classroom Management Strategy
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin challenges the assumption that allowing students to talk freely wastes time or invites misbehavior, arguing instead that teacher-controlled talking breaks are an effective management tool. He identifies three benefits: releasing built-up tension from sustained sitting and concentrating, refocusing students by clearing accumulated boredom before the next lesson, and communicating empathy that students deeply appreciate, since it shows the teacher understands what it is like to sit and listen all day. He notes that talking breaks are especially valuable for students with ADHD and ties the strategy to reciprocity, a key SCM principle in which student goodwill toward the teacher improves listening and motivation. The key, he stresses, is that the teacher controls when and how breaks happen, with expectations taught and modeled beforehand, using transitions or natural breaks in the day as the ideal moment.
points: Teacher-controlled talking breaks are framed as an effective classroom management strategy rather than a waste of time.
Talking breaks release built-up physical and mental tension from extended sitting and concentrating.
A short talking break clears student boredom and 'checked-out' energy so they return more attentive to instruction.
Allowing talk demonstrates empathy, which students appreciate and which triggers the SCM principle of reciprocity.
The strategy only works if the teacher decides when and how breaks happen, with expectations explicitly taught and modeled first.
quotes: It’s common to assume that allowing students to talk to whomever they want about whatever they want is a bad thing.
But when you decide when and how it’s done, it’s nothing of the sort.

Because it effectively releases the natural tension that builds up from sitting and concentrating for long periods of time. It relieves antsiness, restlessness, and excitability, which are major causes of misbehavior.
For most students, talking and sharing with friends is the quickest way to get boredom out of their system. It clears the boards, gets the blood flowing, and frees them to focus on the next lesson.

It shows them that you know what it’s like to be in their shoes and to sit, listen, and learn for an entire school day. It’s this kind of empathy that makes students want to please you and behave for you.
The key to allowing talking breaks is for you to decide when and how they’re done. It’s to teach and model precisely what is and isn’t okay before putting them into practice.
